Human-inspired agentic video understanding via coarse-to-fine spatiotemporal exploration
abstract: Current video understanding models follow a passive perception paradigm, relying on fixed sampling strategies that can introduce substantial temporal redundancy and fine-grained detail loss. We reformulate video understanding as an agentic decision-making process, treating the video as a dynamic environment for active exploration. We propose HIVE (Human-Inspired Video Explorer), a training-free agentic framework driven by a coarse-to-fine spatiotemporal strategy. HIVE first constructs a compact temporal environment by pruning visually redundant segments and augmenting the retained segments with semantic captions, forming a query-ready bimodal memory bank. On top of this abstracted environment, an LLM-based agent executes an iterative Planning-Action-Reasoning-Reflection loop to adaptively determine ''when and where to look.'' Guided by the user query and a global event synopsis, the agent invokes perceptual tools for temporal localization, caption retrieval, active spatial cropping, and localized video VQA, enabling it to select informative temporal moments and inspect question-relevant spatial regions only when necessary. Without task-specific fine-tuning, HIVE achieves 59.1\% accuracy on the long-video subset of Video-MME, 69.6\%/62.1\% on the EgoSchema subset/full benchmark, and 75.8\% on NExT-QA. These results demonstrate that active evidence acquisition provides an efficient alternative to uniformly encoding dense video inputs, improving long-video understanding and fine-grained visual reasoning under limited computational budgets.

title: scikit-fair: A Python package for fairness-aware data preparation
abstract: The growing adoption of machine learning in high-stakes domains has intensified the need for tools that systematically detect and mitigate bias in training data. While fairness-aware pre-processing methods have shown promise, they remain scattered across isolated research repositories, limiting their practical adoption and inclusion in comparative studies. This paper introduces scikit-fair , an open-source Python package that unifies a suite of pre-processing bias mitigation algorithms under a single API, fully compatible with scikit-learn or imbalanced-learn pipelines. The package provides built-in benchmark datasets, a comprehensive metrics module covering several group fairness criteria alongside standard classification measures, and dedicated auditing tools for both data-level and prediction-level bias analysis. Additionally, an experiment orchestration layer enables declarative, reproducible benchmarking across multiple methods, classifiers, and datasets, with automatic generation of publication-ready comparison reports. The package is available on PyPI and is accompanied by comprehensive documentation.

title: Improving adam via tracked gradient centralization and smooth radial correction
From data heterogeneity to convergence: A data-centric review of federated learning
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for data hunger in centralized learning. This paradigm enables privacy with multiple clients to train a shared-task model collaboratively without exposing their local data. While being a key component in any learning system, data is also a primary source of vulnerabilities and challenges, and a major determinant of a stable and well-converged training. Existing FL reviews describe general foundations, security practices, opportunities, challenges, and applications, without delving into diverse aspects of data and considering problems from the data perspective. They rarely provide a data-lens synthesis that links concrete data properties, split protocols, and defenses to convergence speed and stability. This survey fills that gap with three advances. First, we analyze "non-IID" into measurable traits and rank their influence on convergence as strong, medium, or light, explaining the mechanisms behind each and reconciling evidence across images, texts, and graphs. Second, we connect experimental splitting practices to the real phenomena they emulate, expose the artifacts they introduce, and show how those artifacts affect target accuracy. Third, we analyze how data-related vulnerabilities and their proposed defenses affect convergence, reporting performance under clean and adversarial conditions to make the convergence-robustness trade-off explicit. To our knowledge, this is the first survey to provide a complete understanding of data-related challenges that govern FL. With clear takeaways distilled for each concern, our work serves as actionable guidance, helping practitioners design their system with predictable convergence and stability.

title: LumiSpec: Phase-preserving frequency modulation for structure-preserving low-light image enhancement
abstract: Low-light image enhancement requires not only improved visibility, but also reliable preservation of structural cues for downstream machine vision tasks. A central challenge is that existing enhancement methods often fail to effectively balance structure recovery and noise suppression under severe illumination degradation, leading to blurred informative boundaries or unstable high-frequency responses. To address this issue, this paper proposes LumiSpec, a luminance-guided network for structure-preserving low-light image enhancement. First, an asymmetric luminance-guided backbone is designed to allocate most representational capacity to structure restoration, while a lightweight chrominance pathway is retained for efficient color recovery. Second, a Frequency-Domain Amplitude Modulator is introduced into the luminance branch to perform phase-preserving spectral modulation, which recalibrates degraded feature responses while maintaining spatial consistency. Finally, a low-resolution cross-branch interaction module and a patch-wise self-attention module are jointly employed to align luminance and chrominance features and refine local structural details before reconstruction. Extensive experiments on low-light static and real nighttime dynamic scene datasets demonstrate that LumiSpec consistently outperforms competitive state-of-the-art methods from illumination-adjustment, Retinex-based, Transformer-based, and diffusion-based paradigms. In particular, the proposed method improves downstream detection accuracy while maintaining low model complexity and fast inference, supporting its practical deployment as a preprocessing component for image recognition systems.

title: Adversarial evolution of deepfake generation and detection: A systematic review of paradigms, evaluation, and governance
abstract: The rapid advancement of deep generative models has driven deepfake technology to a level of audio-visual realism at which classical detection paradigms exhibit clear degradation, with implications for personal privacy, public trust, and content security. As generation methods continue to outpace detection in fidelity, controllability, and cross-modal coordination, deepfake research is best understood as an adversarial co-evolution between the two sides rather than two separate technical lines. This paper provides a systematic review of deepfake generation and detection from this perspective, analysing how successive generative paradigms render preceding detection methods ineffective and trigger the emergence of new forensic approaches. We partition the 2014-2025 period into three overlapping adversarial cycles defined by the dominant detection cue family: the frequency-cue era, the blending-boundary and deep-representation era, and the semantic and physical-consistency era. For each cycle, we trace how breakthroughs along the parallel GAN, autoencoder, and diffusion routes render the preceding detection paradigm ineffective. We integrate detection performance, generation quality, and cross-modal consistency into a unified three-axis evaluation matrix, and outline a technology-law-ethics governance framework spanning generation-time watermarking, content provenance, and lifecycle risk management. Existing gaps and future research directions are identified to support the responsible development of deepfake-related technologies.

Concurrent training and layer pruning of deep neural networks
abstract: We propose an algorithm capable of identifying and eliminating irrelevant layers of a neural network during the early stages of training. In contrast to weight or filter-level pruning, layer pruning reduces the harder to parallelize sequential computation of a neural network. We employ a structure using linear residual connections around nonlinear network sections that allow the flow of information through the network once a nonlinear section is pruned. Our approach is based on variational inference principles using Gaussian scale mixture priors on the neural network weights and allows for substantial cost savings during both training and inference. More specifically, the variational posterior distribution of scalar Bernoulli random variables multiplying a whole layer weight matrix of its nonlinear sections is learned, similarly to adaptive layer-wise dropout. To overcome challenges of concurrent learning and pruning such as premature pruning and lack of robustness with respect to weight initialization or the size of the starting network, we adopt the “flattening” hyper-prior on the prior parameters. We prove that, as a result of the usage of this hyper-prior, the solutions of the resulting optimization problem always describe deterministic networks with parameters of the posterior distribution at either 0 or 1. We formulate a projected stochastic gradient descent algorithm and prove its convergence to such a solution using well-known stochastic approximation results. In particular, we establish and prove analytically conditions that lead to a layer’s weights converging to zero and derive practical pruning conditions from the theoretical results. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on the MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets and the commonly used fully-connected, convolutional and residual architectures LeNet, VGG16 and ResNet. The simulations demonstrate that our method achieves state-of the-art performance for layer pruning at reduced computational cost in distinction to competing methods due to the concurrent training and pruning.

title: FCM-Hash: Label-enhanced cross-modal hashing via adaptive Mamba fusion and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks

FasTARFlow: Distilling transformer-based autoregressive flows into fast inverse autoregressive models
abstract: TARFlow introduces Transformer-based autoregressive flows that overcome the challenges of expressiveness and training in normalizing flows (NFs), achieving state-of-the-art likelihoods and high-quality samples. However, its autoregressive nature results in slow sampling, which limits its practical applicability. In this work, we propose FasTARFlow, a distillation framework that transfers knowledge from a trained TARFlow model, used as the teacher, to a fast and parallelizable inverse autoregressive flow (IAF) model, used as the student. The distilled model maintains competitive sample quality while substantially accelerating inference. We evaluate FasTARFlow on three datasets spanning a broad range of resolutions and content statistics: AFHQ ( ), FFHQ-256, and CIFAR-100. Experiments show that FasTARFlow achieves sample quality comparable to or better than that of the teacher TARFlow across all three datasets while significantly accelerating sampling. Moreover, FasTARFlow is particularly effective in the high-resolution regime, where the autoregressive sampling cost of TARFlow is most severe. These results advance the practicality of NF-based generative modeling.

title: A survey on assessing the generalization area of neural networks: Uncertainty, out-of-distribution and adversarial samples
abstract:
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in numerous applications. However, determining whether a DNN will produce the correct output for a given input is a non-trivial problem. A DNN is expected to deliver the correct output if the input is within its generalization envelope. In this case, the information contained in the input sample is processed reliably by the network. Assessing at inference time whether a DNN is generalizing correctly is of great practical importance. 
Currently, approaches that try to achieve this goal are investigated rather independently across different problem setups, leading to three main fields of research: predictive uncertainty, out-of-distribution detection, and adversarial example detection. This survey connects these three fields within the broader framework of investigating the generalization performance of machine learning methods, particularly DNNs. We highlight the common ground, point to the most promising approaches, and provide a structured overview of methods that offer a means to establish at inference time if an input is within the generalization envelope of a DNN.

title: Coefficient-space text-guided GAN editing with probability-density geodesic optimization
TADSOB: Enhancing jailbreaking attacks on LLMs via trajectory-aware dynamic suffix optimization with buffer
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of tasks, yet they continue to demonstrate vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. Existing token-level jailbreak attacks, notably the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) method, have proven effective in automatically generating adversarial suffixes that compromise even robustly aligned LLMs. However, current token-level jailbreak strategies suffer from several limitations, including a tendency for the optimization process to get stuck in local minima, slow convergence, and insufficient utilization of internal model information in the attack mechanism. To address these limitations, we propose a Trajectory-Aware Dynamic Suffix Optimization with Buffer (TADSOB) framework to optimize jailbreak suffixes, offering a new way for automated red teaming and enhancing the understanding of jailbreak mechanisms. First, TADSOB incorporates dynamic suffix initialization, which refines the precision of gradient-index-guided token replacement in the sampling phase and improves overall computational efficiency. Second, TADSOB extracts magnitude and angular features from the hidden layers of the target model for suffix components and propose trajectory-guided evaluation metrics to manipulate the model's reasoning pathways, thereby facilitating LLM jailbreaking. Finally, TADSOB maintains a buffer container storing the top-b suffixes with minimal loss for multi-coordinate updates, accelerating loss convergence. Experimental results show that TADSOB achieves state-of-the-art performance on the AdvBench benchmark across multiple target LLMs, achieving up to a 5.8× speedup and an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 82% on Llama-2.

title: Visibility-guided geometry memory network for neural multi-view depth inference
DMBS: A band-limited Gaussian noise cancellation algorithm based on a diffusion model and Bhattacharyya step-number guidance
abstract: The spectral overlap between band-limited gaussian noise and the target signal severely degrades the efficacy of conventional filtering methods, posing a significant challenge in the field of signal processing. Recently, diffusion models (DMs) have offered a novel perspective for gaussian white noise cancellation via the synergistic mechanism of their forward noise addition and reverse denoising processes. However, the standard Gaussian white noise assumption presents a fundamental physical mismatch with the actual characteristics of band-limited gaussian noise after receiver front-end filtering and channel equalisation. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an band-limited gaussian noise cancellation algorithm based on a diffusion model and Bhattacharyya step-number guidance (DMBS). Theoretically, subject to a non-identity covariance matrix, this paper fundamentally reconstructs the probability transition state equations and the closed-form expression of the loss function, establishing a generalised diffusion denoising theoretical framework tailored for band-limited gaussian noise. Algorithmically, the Bhattacharyya distance is introduced to quantify statistical deviations, enabling a step-number guidance mechanism that achieves precise alignment between the observed signal and the denoising trajectory. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that DMBS consistently outperforms benchmark methods, including Wiener filtering, the denoising and classification network (DNCNet), and channel denoising diffusion models (CDDM), in terms of both mean squared error (MSE) and bit error rate (BER). In particular, under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, DMBS achieves an equivalent SNR gain of nearly 10 dB at the same BER level.

title: A MONAI-based software framework for architecture–task analysis in 3D medical image segmentation
Inconsistency-aware frequency fusion and region–boundary refinement for RGB–thermal camouflaged object detection
abstract: Camouflaged object detection (COD) aims to segment objects whose appearance and structural patterns closely resemble their surroundings. RGB-thermal (RGB-T) pairs provide complementary visible and thermal cues, but their local responses are often inconsistent around ambiguous regions and weak boundaries. Uniform cross-modal fusion may therefore transfer unreliable modality responses into the prediction. This paper presents IFRB-Net, an inconsistency-aware RGB-T COD framework that learns reliability-adaptive features through frequency-level fusion, hard-region modulation, and coupled region-boundary decoding. First, the Cross-Modal Frequency Fusion module decomposes modality-specific features into wavelet subbands and uses Hilbert phase-guided competitive weighting to emphasize locally reliable structural evidence. Second, the Hard-Region Discrepancy Enhancement module learns a discrepancy-uncertainty gate from cross-modal differences, gradient inconsistency, and coarse prediction uncertainty to modulate ambiguous regions before decoding. Third, the Region-Boundary Bidirectional Refinement Decoder couples region and boundary streams so that object completeness and contour localization are refined collaboratively. Experiments on six public RGB-T benchmarks show that IFRB-Net performs favorably against representative single-modal and multi-modal camouflaged-object and salient-object detection methods. Additional ablation, robustness, and feature visualization analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed inconsistency-aware fusion-and-refinement strategy.

FracTrace: Long-horizon credit assignment in deep reinforcement learning via fractional eligibility traces
abstract: Temporal credit assignment becomes intractable when reward signals are displaced hundreds of steps from causal actions, limiting learning in robotic manipulation, autonomous navigation, and long-horizon planning. Conventional exponentially-decaying eligibility traces allocate negligible credit beyond moderate horizons, as their geometric forgetting renders causal attribution effectively impossible at extended lags. This paper introduces FracTrace, a Fractional Trace Actor-Critic framework that replaces exponential decay with power-law memory kernels derived from fractional calculus. Variable-order Mittag-Leffler functions are incorporated at two architectural levels: hierarchical traces maintain multi-timescale state representations across fast, medium, and slow dynamics, while fractional eligibility traces induce algebraic decay that sustains meaningful credit assignment on tasks with reward delays of 500–800 steps. A key design principle retains the standard distributional Bellman operator for the critic, preserving -contraction in Wasserstein metric, while fractionalization is applied exclusively to policy-side advantages. For an idealized policy-gradient variant of the algorithm, almost-sure convergence of the critic to the true value function and of the policy to a stationary point neighborhood of radius , a truncation-dependent bias term, are established under two-timescale stochastic approximation, where vanishes as the truncation horizon ; the practical algorithm uses the PPO clipped surrogate and is evaluated empirically. The critic achieves sample complexity , matching classical actor-critic rates while capturing substantially longer dependencies. Empirical evaluation across six long-horizon tasks demonstrates substantial improvements over PPO, PPO-LSTM, R2D2, and GTrXL, with FracTrace uniquely solving extreme-horizon tasks (800 steps) at per-step complexity. The kernel-swap ablation, which isolates kernel choice within an otherwise identical architecture, supports the conclusion that these gains stem from power-law memory structure; the PPO-LSTM comparison provides converging evidence at the level of a full baseline architecture rather than a single-factor control.

When financial fine-tuning fails: A three-level detectability analysis of numerical hallucination in domain-adapted language models
abstract: Financial large language models are increasingly deployed for summarization of reports and disclosures, where numerical hallucination poses significant practical risks. While prior work often attributes such hallucination to insufficient numerical reasoning, this assumption has not been systematically tested under controlled fine-tuning settings. In this paper, we conduct a cost-effective, controlled study of numerical hallucination in financial summarization across three model variants: a base instruction-tuned model, a domain language-adapted model (FT-A), and a numeracy-enhanced domain model (FT-A+B+C). We introduce a three-level detectability taxonomy distinguishing between overt hallucination (currency-denominated fabrication), covert-explicit hallucination (professional-convention numbers), and covert-implicit hallucination (ungrounded quantitative claims). Our results reveal that domain fine-tuning substantially degrades numerical restraint at all detectability levels. While the Base model maintains near-zero hallucination rates (5.4\%), FT-A exhibits 82.5\% overt hallucination and FT-A+B+C reaches 98\%. Contrary to intuition, numeracy supervision amplifies rather than mitigates hallucination across all levels. We identify template injection---the insertion of memorized canonical values regardless of input content---as a primary hallucination mechanism in fine-tuned models. These findings demonstrate that numerical hallucination in financial summarization is driven by the degradation of numerical restraint through domain adaptation, not by insufficient numerical reasoning. We recommend that evaluation protocols assess hallucination across all detectability levels and that deployment practices include explicit mechanisms for grounding-aware generation or abstention.

Comprehensive survey of sign language recognition and its future through computer vision
abstract: Over the past three decades, the focus of research in sign language recognition (SLR) and sign language translation (SLT) has shifted significantly. Early research relied primarily on wearable hardware sensing solutions such as wired data gloves and electromagnetic trackers, while the current trend has shifted to data-driven, vision-based deep learning frameworks such as 3D convolutional neural networks (3D-CNNs) and label-free pose estimation have been extremely helpful. This article attempts to review the evolution of SLR and translation over the past thirty years, focusing primarily on Australian Sign Language (Auslan). The article will explore how foundational technologies have evolved into specialized models where they address the unique challenges of sign language, using models such as SAM-SLR and SignVTCL. Finally, the article will discuss some problems with current evaluation methods. A significant issue is the large performance gap between recognizing individual gestures and recognizing consecutive sentences. One issue is co-articulation which refers to signs influence on each other when produced in sequence, causing assimilations or drops that puzzle recognition models. Another is the presence of non-manual signals (facial expressions, head movements) which carry crucial grammatical information (questions, negation, etc.) but are not explicitly annotated in gloss sequences. In addition, the differences in speech rate and style among sign language interpreters are substantial; for example, the speech rate in news videos is much faster than in the lab dataset, posing a significant challenge to the model's time alignment capabilities. Furthermore, currently used word-translation-based evaluation criteria struggle to fully reflect the rich meaning of Auslan.

Interval-based label enhancement via principal component alignment
abstract: Label distribution learning addresses label polysemy, but acquiring precise label distributions is expensive. Label enhancement mitigates this by converting low-cost binary logical labels into continuous label distributions, reducing the reliance on fine-grained annotation. Conventional enhancement methods, however, rely on discriminative loss functions that drive scores toward discrete extremes ( or ), compromising the fidelity and continuity of recovered distributions. We propose ILE-PCA, which generates unnormalized label scores via logic-constrained target generation: for a logical , the target is drawn from ; for a logical , from . This avoids the misleading guidance of discriminative losses. To align scores with the intrinsic structure of true distributions, we apply PCA to the logical label matrix and enforce alignment between its dominant subspace and the generated scores. Experiments show that ILE-PCA excels in label distribution recovery, achieving the best average rank across datasets and outperforming all compared state-of-the-art methods in the majority of cases.

title: Co-Debater: A multimodal dialectical reasoning framework for suppressing reasoning hallucinations in hateful meme detection
Online learning extreme learning machine with low-complexity predictive plasticity rule and FPGA implementation
abstract: This work reports a simplified, biologically inspired predictive local learning rule that eliminates the need for global backpropagation in conventional neural networks and membrane integration in neuromorphic computing. Weight updates are triggered only on prediction errors and are performed using sparse, binary-driven vector additions. We integrate this rule into an extreme learning machine (ELM), replacing the conventional computationally intensive matrix inversion. Compared to standard ELM, our approach reduces training complexity from to in terms of hidden-layer nodes, while maintaining comparable accuracy averaged across different training and test datasets. We validate performance on various open-source and in-house-collected datasets under strong noise and class imbalance. We also demonstrate a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) implementation and compare it with prior studies, showing significant reductions in computational and memory requirements and higher throughput. This design demonstrates strong potential for energy-efficient online learning on low-cost edge devices.

Second-order predefined-time neural networks for sparse recovery
abstract: Sparse signal recovery from limited linear measurements is a fundamental problem in compressive sensing and related inverse problems. It remains challenging due to its combinatorial nature and the lack of algorithms with guaranteed or explicitly controllable convergence times. In order to deal with this issue, in this paper, we study the continuous time neural dynamic approaches for solving the l0-norm sparse recovery problem. First, by modifying the WBP function, we give a smoothing approximation of the l0-norm, and then develop a convex relaxation of the sparse optimization problem. Second, by introducing the sliding technique, we propose a second-order time-varying predefined-time neurodynamic approach. And then we give some theoretical analysis, such as model equivalence, solution existence and predefined-time convergence. Third, a discrete-time counterpart of the proposed neural network is further derived, which is shown to inherit the predefined-time convergence in the sense of discrete time. Moreover, we develop a delayed second-order neurodynamic system and investigate its asymptotic stability. Finally, numerical experiments on sparse recovery and feature selection demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

COTET: Cross-view optimal transport for knowledge graph entity typing
abstract: Knowledge graph entity typing (KGET) aims to infer missing entity type instances in knowledge graphs. Previous research has predominantly centered around leveraging contextual information associated with entities, which provides valuable clues for inference. However, they have long ignored the dual nature of information inherent in entities, encompassing both high-level coarse-grained cluster knowledge and fine-grained type knowledge. This paper introduces Cross-view Optimal Transport for knowledge graph Entity Typing (COTET), a method that effectively incorporates the information on how types are clustered into the representation of entities and types. COTET comprises three modules: i) Multi-view Generation and Encoder, which captures structured knowledge at different levels of granularity through entity-type, entity-cluster, and type-cluster-type perspectives; ii) Cross-view Optimal Transport, transporting view-specific embeddings to a unified space by minimizing the Wasserstein distance from a distributional alignment perspective; iii) Pooling-based Entity Typing Prediction, employing a mixture pooling mechanism to aggregate prediction scores from diverse neighbors of an entity. Additionally, we introduce a distribution-based loss function to mitigate the occurrence of false negatives during training. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of COTET when compared to existing baselines.

RS-OVD: Region-semantic stabilization for open-vocabulary object detection
abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) aims to localize and recognize objects described by arbitrary category names, including classes that are not annotated during detector training. Despite the progress achieved by vision-language pretraining, existing OVD methods still face three practical challenges: unstable region-level semantic alignment, high-confidence false positives from semantically similar backgrounds, and performance degradation when new categories are introduced incrementally. To address these issues, this paper proposes RS-OVD, a region-semantic stabilization framework for robust open-vocabulary detection under both static and dynamically expanding vocabularies. The proposed method learns a unified region embedding space in which object queries are aligned with category semantics while preserving local visual discrimination. To strengthen positive region representation, RS-OVD integrates category-level textual guidance, cropped-object semantic consistency, and region-level structural constraints into the training objective. To refine the negative decision boundary, a margin-based hard negative suppression strategy is designed to identify background proposals with low spatial overlap but high semantic similarity to category prototypes, thereby reducing high-confidence false detections caused by contextual or visually similar regions. Furthermore, for incremental open-world scenarios, memory replay and parameter stabilization are incorporated to maintain old-category knowledge while adapting to newly added categories with limited annotations. Extensive experiments on COCO and LVIS demonstrate that RS-OVD improves seen-category detection, novel-category generalization, rare-category robustness, and continual adaptation. On COCO, RS-OVD achieves 60.4 Seen AP, 42.3 Novel AP, 58.6 AP50, and 47.6 AP75, showing stronger generalization to held-out categories while preserving accurate object localization. On LVIS, it obtains 35.8 AP and 26.2 APr, with consistent gains across common and frequent categories, indicating improved robustness under large-vocabulary and long-tailed conditions. These results suggest that explicitly stabilizing region-semantic representations and suppressing semantically similar background responses provide an effective route for reliable open-vocabulary object detection. Code and models are available at https://github.com/1colorworker/RS-OVD.git.

title: A fast low-rank two-factor formulation for symmetric doubly stochastic clustering
abstract: Doubly stochastic similarities are useful in clustering because they balance node degrees and often yield clearer block structure. Their main drawback is cost: direct formulations work with a dense $n\times n$ similarity matrix. One-factor low-rank models of the form $W=UU^\top, U\in\R_+^{n\times r}$ reduce the storage to $\mathcal{O}(nr)$ for $r\ll n$, but the factor update is still self-coupled. We propose DSD2F, a two-factor formulation with $W=UV^\top$. A quadratic penalty keeps the two factors close, and an augmented-Lagrangian treatment of the row-sum constraint gives projected closed-form updates for $U$ and $V$. The method therefore keeps the $\mathcal{O}(nr)$ storage profile of low-rank approaches without optimizing a dense graph variable. On 10 benchmark datasets, DSD2F attains the best average RI rank, gives the highest RI on 6 datasets, and is noticeably faster than the other low-rank baselines on larger problems.

title: TabLlama: Hierarchical transformer for predicting ballistic vehicle arrival scenario in complex temporal tabular data
A min–max manifold regularization framework for multi-view clustering
abstract: Integration of manifold learning (i.e., local geometric structure learning) with clustering has been found effective for correctly identifying subgroups in the data. The manifold learning problem becomes more challenging in a multi-view data setting, as data represented across multiple views may be sampled from different underlying manifolds. Learning an accurate manifold can significantly improve the performance of multi-view data clustering. We propose a novel multi-view manifold learning algorithm using min–max operators. This ‘Min-Max Manifold’ is embedded within a proposed NMF-based framework designed to learn consensus information from multi-view data and preserve it in a low-rank representation. In contrast to deep multi-view clustering methods that enforce latent-space alignment, our method directly constructs a parameter-free consensus manifold that preserves majority-consistent geometric structure while retaining essential complementary information. Our framework further incorporates a kernel-based diversity constraint to better exploit view-specific complementary information when constructing the consensus representation and imposes an orthogonality constraint to make the learned consensus representation directly clustering-oriented. Extensive experimental results and visualizations show the effectiveness of the proposed method in finding accurate clusters and its superiority over other state-of-the-art methods.

Sample-centric adversarial masking for robust multimodal learning under missing modalities
abstract: Multimodal learning achieves strong performance by integrating complementary information from diverse sources, but its effectiveness often deteriorates when modalities are missing due to practical constraints such as hardware limitations, heterogeneous data collection protocols, and privacy regulations. Recent studies have recognized that robustness varies across missing-modality combinations; however, most existing approaches adopt a modality-centric perspective, where vulnerable cases are defined primarily by modality types. This view overlooks sample-level heterogeneity, in which prediction difficulty can differ substantially across samples even under the same modality availability, and it becomes increasingly impractical as the number of possible missing-modality combinations grows exponentially with the number of modalities. To address these limitations, we propose SAMA ( S ample- A ware M asking with A dversarial training), a sample-centric framework that integrates sample-specific adversarial masking with knowledge distillation to identify vulnerable missing-modality patterns at the instance level, efficiently exploring challenging missing scenarios without exhaustive enumeration, and improving average robustness in the large majority of missing-modality conditions across three benchmarks.

title: Parameter-efficient multi-position illumination guidance for low-light image enhancement
CroSSFed: Prototype-guided server-side finetuning with client-server reweighting for cross-domain semi-supervised federated learning
abstract: Semi-supervised Federated Learning is a form of distributed deep learning in which multiple data centers (clients) collaboratively train a shared neural network under the coordination of a central server. The training process is performed without the exchange of private data and utilizes a mix of labeled and mostly unlabeled data. In the labels-at-server context, the server has a small, labeled dataset, while the participating clients possess no labels at all. Thus, there is a risk of server domain bias during server-side training, particularly in common real-world scenarios in which the server and client data come from different domains and thus have different distributions. To address this issue, the present study proposes a Prototype-Guided Server Finetuning mechanism that uses client prototypes to guide the update of the server model during the training process in such a way as to prevent overfitting to the server domain. A Client-Server Reweighting mechanism is additionally proposed to combine the client-aggregated model and the fine-tuned server model dynamically as training proceeds such that the client-aggregated model is gradually assigned increasing importance, thereby further decreasing the server domain bias. The experimental results obtained on a CIFAR10 -CINIC10 dataset show that the proposed method, designated as CroSSFed, achieves a 7\% improvement in the classification accuracy over the state-of-the-art SemiFl method, which considers a similar data arrangement but does not address the cross-domain scenario.

SigID: Signature-based open-set face identification without additional training
abstract: Open-set face identification (OSFI) requires not only correct identification of enrolled identities but also reliable rejection of unseen individuals. We propose SigID (Signature-based open-set face IDentification), a lightweight and training-free framework that models identity through soft relational signatures derived from embeddings of pre-trained face recognition models. Unlike existing ranking-based methods that rely on rigid rank ordering or handcrafted matching rules, SigID captures stable neighbourhood structure by aggregating highly related identities, making it less sensitive to score perturbations and more consistent across varying conditions. At inference time, probe and gallery signatures are compared using a simple compatibility function combined with cosine similarity in a two-stage decision process. The framework is architecture-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and introduces minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and backbones demonstrate that SigID consistently improves open-set identification performance at low-FAR (most-secure) operating points. When combined with NAC, SigID achieves up to 53% DIR@FAR gains over cosine similarity at FAR=0.1, while also improving NAC itself by 10% to 27% and maintaining strong generalization across the evaluated settings.
